nameStory: The broad-winged tree cricket gets its name from having noticeably wider wings compared to its close relatives like the narrow-winged tree cricket. These delicate insects spend most of their lives in trees and shrubs, where their musical chirping fills warm summer evenings. The 'broad wings' are actually the male's sound-producing structures, making them nature's tiny violinists.
description: Broad-winged tree crickets are slender, pale green to whitish insects about the size of your thumbnail. Unlike the chunky ground crickets you might find under rocks, these delicate creatures have long, thread-like antennae and translucent wings that shimmer in the light. Males are the musicians of the species, using their wings to create the sweet, continuous trills you hear on warm summer nights. They're built for life in the trees, with long legs perfect for navigating through leaves and stems.

idTips.label: Wing width
idTips.description: Males have distinctly broad, translucent wings that overlap when folded, feeling papery to the touch and often appearing slightly wider than the insect's body

idTips.label: Body color
idTips.description: Pale green to creamy white coloration that may appear almost translucent, with a soft, smooth texture when gently handled

idTips.label: Antennae length
idTips.description: Extremely long, hair-thin antennae that extend well beyond the body length and feel delicate like fine thread when touched

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Slender body about 12-15mm long with long, spindly legs that feel fragile and are perfectly adapted for climbing through vegetation

idTips.label: Song pattern
idTips.description: Males produce a continuous, musical trill rather than the choppy chirps of ground crickets - a sweet, high-pitched sound that can last for minutes

habitat: Look for broad-winged tree crickets in deciduous trees and tall shrubs throughout New England's forests, parks, and wooded suburban areas. They particularly favor oak, maple, and fruit trees, where they feed on aphids and soft plant material. You'll find them from sea level up to moderate elevations, especially in areas with mixed hardwood forests and forest edges.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active. Eggs laid the previous fall are developing in tree bark and plant stems, invisible to casual observers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time! Adults emerge in mid to late summer and are most easily found by following their continuous trilling songs on warm evenings after sunset.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, with males continuing to sing until the first hard frosts. Females lay eggs in tree bark during this time before dying.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity. Eggs overwinter in protected crevices in bark and stems, waiting for warm weather to hatch into the next generation.

funFact: Male broad-winged tree crickets are living thermometers - you can calculate the temperature in Fahrenheit by counting their chirps for 15 seconds and adding 40, giving you an accuracy within a few degrees!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the narrow-winged tree cricket, but the broad-winged species has noticeably wider wings that extend beyond the sides of the body when folded. Memory trick: 'Broad wings, broad sound' - the broad-winged species produces a more continuous, fuller trill compared to the more intermittent calls of narrow-winged tree crickets.
contextualKnowledge: Tree crickets are often called 'thermometer crickets' because of their temperature-dependent singing rate, making them surprisingly accurate natural weather instruments. Unlike ground crickets that are often considered garden pests, tree crickets are actually beneficial insects that help control aphid populations.
compareHints: Among New England's tree crickets, the broad-winged species is distinguished by its wider male wings compared to the narrow-winged tree cricket, and its preference for deciduous trees rather than the pine-loving pine tree cricket. The snowy tree cricket is similar in color but smaller and has different wing proportions, while the black-horned tree cricket has distinctive dark markings on its antennae that the broad-winged species lacks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's tree crickets, this species stands out for its narrow wing shape compared to the broad-winged tree cricket's obviously wider wings.

Among New England's tree crickets, Pine Tree Cricket is unique in its exclusive preference for pine trees - Snowy Tree Crickets prefer deciduous trees and shrubs, while Broad-winged Tree Crickets favor fruit trees and berry bushes.
Among New England's tree crickets, the Black-horned is the easiest to identify thanks to its dark antennae.
Among New England's tree crickets, the snowy tree cricket has the palest, most translucent appearance.
Among New England's tree crickets, the Four-spotted is the only one with exactly four dark spots on its body.
